We begin by “translating” the relationships into their meaning. (Remember that each person is given a letter; for example, Amber = h means her “code‐letter” is h.) From the given relationships we can deduce the following:

• “Amber = h  the child of Bryan = h”
  This tells us that Amber (h) is the child of Bryan. (Bryan’s “code‐letter” is given on his own line.)

• “Bryan = t  the child of Christina = v”
  So Bryan’s code‐letter is t and – reading the child phrase – the child of Christina is the person whose code is v.

• “Christina = y  the child of Felicia = s”
  Thus Christina’s code‐letter is y and the child of Felicia is the person with code s.

• “Dana = s  the enemy of Amber = v”
  Since Dana’s code‐letter is s, and the enemy of Amber is the person whose code is v.

• “Elizabeth = v  the enemy of Bryan = y”
  Elizabeth’s code‐letter is v. Also, Bryan’s enemy is the person whose code is y.

• “Felicia = q  the enemy of Christina = t”
  Felicia is tagged with q while Christina’s enemy is the person whose code is t.

In our “mapping” the parent‐child relationships are:
 – Bryan is the parent of Amber (since Amber’s code h matches “the child of Bryan = h”).
 – Christina is the parent of the person with code v. We see that Elizabeth = v, so Christina is Elizabeth’s parent.
 – Felicia is the parent of the person with code s. Dana = s, so Felicia is Dana’s parent.

Now, the question we must answer is:
  Who is the friend of the child of Christina?

Step 1. Identify the child of Christina.
  From “the child of Christina = v” and “Elizabeth = v”, we see that the child of Christina is Elizabeth.

Step 2. Identify the friend of the child.
  In many puzzles of this style a “friend” is defined in a way that is analogous to the parent/child or enemy relationships that we see listed. (Notice how the “parent” of Amber was given by Bryan’s code letter ‘t’.) In a parallel manner the puzzle instructs us to “read” the relationship carefully to extract the designated code‐letter. In our example explanation the only step given was:
   “the parent of Amber = t”
which produced the answer “t”.

Likewise, by the same “reading procedure” we now “read” the clue:
  “the friend of the child of Christina”
Since we have already established that the child of Christina is Elizabeth (whose code is v), the intended “reading” directs us to the piece of information that names the “friend” of the person coded v. (Notice that in the enemy relations we have items like “the enemy of Amber = v” or “the enemy of Bryan = y”. In like fashion the friend relation is meant to be read from the notation.)

Step 3. Recognize that only one letter has so far not been “assigned” as a relation on the friend/enemy side in the same style as in the example. By a process of elimination the answer (in the same “reading style” as in step 1) is given by the letter that has not already been “used” as a relation end‐point. Here the only letter that remains available to serve as the code for the friend of Elizabeth is “q.”

Thus, following the same format as the example we state:
  the friend of the child of Christina = q

So the answer is q

From the information given, we first identify who the child of Christina is. Looking at the second line:

  “Bryan = t  the child of Christina = v”

we see that the child of Christina is identified by v. Then, matching the letters with their names from the first parts of the lines we have:

  Amber = h  
  Bryan = t  
  Christina = y  
  Dana = s  
  Elizabeth = v  
  Felicia = q  

So the child of Christina (v) is Elizabeth.

Next, we need to find the enemy of Elizabeth. We are provided enemy relationships on the other lines. Notice line 4:

  “Dana = s  the enemy of Amber = v”

This tells us the enemy of Amber is v (Elizabeth). Because enemy relationships are reciprocal (if A is the enemy of B, then B is the enemy of A), it follows that Elizabeth’s enemy is Amber.

Since Amber is associated with the letter h, we conclude:

  the enemy of the child of Christina = h

So the answer is h.

Interpreting the statements step‐by‐step, we note the following key enemy relationships:

• “the enemy of Amber = v” tells us that Amber’s enemy is the person whose letter is v.
  Looking at the list, Elizabeth has the letter v:

Thus, the enemy of Amber is Elizabeth.

Since “enemy” is understood to work both ways (if A is the enemy of B then B is the enemy of A), we deduce that Elizabeth’s enemy is Amber.

Now we tackle the question “Who is the enemy of the enemy of Amber?” By the work just done:

1. The enemy of Amber is v (Elizabeth).
2. Under the assumption that the enemy relation is mutual, the enemy of v (Elizabeth) is Amber.
3. Amber is identified by the letter h (since Amber = h).

So the answer is h

We start with the facts given. In the relationships the “child” facts are stated as follows:

• “the child of Felicia = s”  
  Dana = s

This tells us that Dana is the child of Felicia; that is, Felicia is Dana’s parent.

Next, we need to find “the enemy of the parent of Dana.” Since we just found that the parent of Dana is Felicia, we now must determine Felicia’s enemy.

Looking at the enemy relationships provided we have:

• “the enemy of Amber = v”  (Amber’s enemy is the person whose letter is v)  
• “the enemy of Bryan = y”  (Bryan’s enemy is the person whose letter is y)  
• “the enemy of Christina = t”  (Christina’s enemy is the person whose letter is t)

The information given provides enemy relationships for Amber, Bryan, and Christina. There is no enemy statement given for Felicia. Therefore no enemy is defined for Felicia.

Thus we record the answer in the same format as the example:

1. the parent of Dana = Felicia  
2. the enemy of Felicia is not defined

So the answer is not defined.

(Note that “enemy” and “child” relationships are given; in this puzzle the only “friend” we can identify is the one tied to a given relationship. In our puzzle the only way to “find” a friend is to use an established connection. In our solution we take “the friend of Elizabeth” to be her parent – since every person except Felicia has both a family tie (child of someone) and an “enemy” tie, it turns out that the one “missing” enemy‐relationship from Elizabeth is replaced by a friendship with her parent.) 

We know from the clues that:
• “Bryan’s enemy = y” and “Christina’s enemy = t.” In fact the enemy relationships given pair Bryan and Christina as enemies.
• From “the child of Christina = v” we see that Elizabeth – whose identifier is v – is the child of Christina.

Since Elizabeth is the child of Christina, we can take Christina to be a friend of Elizabeth. (That is, Elizabeth “counts” her parent Christina as her friend.) 

Now:
1. The friend of Elizabeth = Christina.
2. The enemy of Christina = t.

So the answer is t.

Christina is the friend of Elizabeth (since Elizabeth’s enemy is Bryan, and the enemy of Bryan is Christina), and the parent of Christina is Felicia, whose letter is q.

  "Who is the parent of Amber?
  1. the parent of Amber = t

Now let’s explain how to find the answer for:

  "Who is the enemy of the enemy of Elizabeth?"

Step 1. Identify the enemy relationships given. The enemy relations provided are:
  • “the enemy of Amber = v” – meaning the person represented by letter v is the enemy of Amber.
  • “the enemy of Bryan = y” – meaning the person represented by letter y is the enemy of Bryan.
  • “the enemy of Christina = t” – meaning the person represented by letter t is the enemy of Christina.

Step 2. Notice that among the six people each person is assigned a letter:
  Amber = h
  Bryan = t
  Christina = y
  Dana = s
  Elizabeth = v
  Felicia = q

Step 3. Determine the enemy pair that involves Elizabeth. Although we are not directly told “the enemy of Elizabeth”, we see in the enemy statements that the letter v appears as the enemy of Amber (“the enemy of Amber = v”). And since Elizabeth is the one with letter v, we conclude:
  Elizabeth is enemy to Amber.

Step 4. In the enemy statements of other pairs (Bryan and Christina), the enemy relation is mutual. That is, since “the enemy of Bryan = y” and Christina is y, and also “the enemy of Christina = t” and Bryan is t, we infer that enemy relationships work in both directions.

Step 5. Hence if Elizabeth is enemy of Amber then, by the mutual nature of “enemy,” Amber is enemy of Elizabeth.

Step 6. Now, the question “Who is the enemy of the enemy of Elizabeth?” asks us to take the enemy of Elizabeth – which we have found to be Amber – and then determine who is the enemy of that person. We already know:
  “The enemy of Amber = v”
Since v represents Elizabeth, it follows that the enemy of Amber is Elizabeth.

Step 7. Thus, the enemy of the enemy of Elizabeth is Elizabeth itself.

So the answer is v

1. Identify the parent‐child pairs using the numbers on the right. From the three statements about “the child of …”, we pair the person on the left with the person whose letter appears on the right in the matching parent’s statement. 
 • “Amber = h  the child of Bryan = h” tells us that Amber is the child of Bryan.
 • “Bryan = t  the child of Christina = v” and “Christina = y  the child of Felicia = s” are set up by using the letters that appear on the right of the “child of” phrases paired with the left‐side assignments. However, note that each person’s own left–side letter is fixed and unique:
  – Amber’s letter is h.
  – Bryan’s letter is t.
  – Christina’s letter is y.
  – Dana’s letter is s.
  – Elizabeth’s letter is v.
  – Felicia’s letter is q.
 When we match the parent–child relationships by replacing the letter in the “child of” clause with the person whose left–side letter is that letter, we find that:
  – The statement “the child of Christina = v” tells us that the child whose letter is v is the child of Christina. Since Elizabeth’s letter is v, Elizabeth is the child of Christina.
2. Now, determine who is the enemy of the parent of Elizabeth. We know from step 1 that Elizabeth’s parent is Christina.
3. Look at the enemy relationships. The enemy relationships are given by the other three statements. In particular:
 • “Felicia = q  the enemy of Christina = t” tells us that the enemy of Christina has the letter t.
 Since Bryan’s letter is t, Bryan is the enemy of Christina.
4. Therefore, the enemy of the parent of Elizabeth is Bryan, whose letter is t.

So the answer is t

We start by “translating” the statement‐pairs. (Review the example: “the parent of Amber” was solved by noting that the person with Amber’s “child‐mark” is Bryan, whose own mark is t.) Now we interpret the six given statements as follows:

• Line 1: “Amber = h  the child of Bryan = h”
  This tells us that Amber is the child of Bryan.

• Line 2: “Bryan = t  the child of Christina = v”
  Although Bryan’s own mark is t, this line tells us that some person (marked v) is the child of Christina.
  Later we see that “Elizabeth = v” so this means that Elizabeth is the child of Christina.

• Line 3: “Christina = y  the child of Felicia = s”
  That is, Christina has mark y, and some person (marked s) is Felicia’s child.

• Line 4: “Dana = s  the enemy of Amber = v”
  So Dana (s) is Felicia’s child (since Felicia’s child has mark s), and also “the enemy of Amber” carries mark v.

• Line 5: “Elizabeth = v  the enemy of Bryan = y”
  So Elizabeth is v (which we already used as the child of Christina), and Bryan’s enemy is marked y.
  (Notice Bryan’s enemy is the person with mark y – and Christina is y.)

• Line 6: “Felicia = q  the enemy of Christina = t”
  That is, Felicia carries mark q and Christina’s enemy is marked t.
  (We already know that Bryan carries t so Bryan and Christina are enemies.)

Let’s now “read” the question step‐by‐step:

 • QUESTION: “Who is the parent of the friend of the child of Christina?”

Step 1. Identify the “child of Christina.”
 From line 2 we noted that “the child of Christina = v” and since Elizabeth = v, we conclude:
  – The child of Christina is Elizabeth.

Step 2. Identify the “friend” of that child.
 We already know one enemy pair from line 4:
  – “the enemy of Amber = v.” That is, the person marked v is the enemy of Amber.
  Since Elizabeth is v, she is the enemy of Amber.
 Since friend and enemy appear as the two opposite “sides” in these puzzles, the friend of a person is not her enemy.
 Thus the friend of Elizabeth must be someone other than Amber.
 Now examine the established enemy pairs:
  – Amber and Elizabeth are enemies.
  – Bryan and Christina are enemies.
 There is no “enemy” tag on Dana.
 Also, notice from line 4 that Dana = s and from line 3 that “the child of Felicia = s.”
 That tells us Dana is Felicia’s child.
 The only “side‐step” pairing (and the one not involved in any enemy relation with Elizabeth) is Dana.
 Thus it is natural to take:
  – The friend of Elizabeth (the child of Christina) is Dana.

Step 3. Identify the parent of Dana.
 From line 3 we have “the child of Felicia = s” and line 4 tells us Dana = s.
 Thus Dana is Felicia’s child.
 So the parent of Dana is Felicia.

Step 4. Answer using the mark for Felicia.
 From line 6 we know that Felicia = q.

Therefore, “the parent of the friend of the child of Christina” is q.

So the answer is q.

1. First, we determine who is the enemy of Amber. In the statement “Dana = s   the enemy of Amber = v” the enemy of Amber is indicated by the letter v. Looking for who has v as the primary letter, we see “Elizabeth = v   the enemy of Bryan = y”. Thus, the enemy of Amber is Elizabeth.

2. Next, we find the parent of Elizabeth. Although there isn’t an explicit “child of …” line for Elizabeth’s name, notice that in “Bryan = t   the child of Christina = v” the child of Christina is given as v. Since Elizabeth’s primary letter is v, we deduce that Elizabeth is the child of Christina. This shows that the parent of the enemy of Amber is Christina.

3. Now, we identify the enemy of Christina. In “Felicia = q   the enemy of Christina = t” the enemy of Christina is noted as t. Then we look for the person whose primary letter is t, and from “Bryan = t   the child of Christina = v” we see that Bryan’s primary letter is t.

So the answer is t

We are given six people along with “role‐letters” and two kinds of relations. For example, note that the very first line

  Amber = h  the child of Bryan = h

tells us that because the child of Bryan is “h” and Amber is “h”, Amber is Bryan’s child.

The other six “clues” set up a network of parent–child and enemy–enemy relationships. (They are given in a “two‐per line” format.) For instance, one clue is

  Elizabeth = v  the enemy of Bryan = y

which tells us that the enemy of Bryan is the person whose letter is y. (In a later clue we see “Christina = y”, so Bryan’s enemy is Christina.) In another clue

  Felicia = q  the enemy of Christina = t

since Christina’s enemy is the person whose letter is t and we already know “Bryan = t” from another clue, Bryan is the enemy of Christina.

The question we now wish to answer is:

  Who is the enemy of the child of the friend of Bryan?

One may “chain‐substitute” such puzzles in steps. (The example in the problem shows how to “chain‐substitute” the relationship “the parent of Amber” to get Bryan’s letter t.) In our problem the starting link is “friend of Bryan.” Although no “friend” relation is given explicitly, the usual puzzle “trick” is to obtain a friend by “inverting” an enemy relation. In this puzzle the enemy relations are mutual (if A is the enemy of B then B is the enemy of A). Since we know Bryan’s enemy is the person whose letter is y (from “Elizabeth = v the enemy of Bryan = y”) and since we also have “Christina = y”, it follows that Christina is Bryan’s enemy. (Enemies “come in pairs”.) That leaves the remaining people as Bryan’s “friend‐set”. Out of these the network is built by parent–child connections. Notice that Felicia is the parent of Christina (“Christina = y the child of Felicia = s” with Dana = s also present – but the only child–parent assignment we can use that leads to an answer is the one from Felicia). In fact, one may “pick out” Felicia as Bryan’s friend (she is not named as an enemy of Bryan) and her child is given by

  the child of Felicia = s

and we read from the same line that

  Dana = s

so Dana is Felicia’s child. (That is, Dana is the child of the friend of Bryan.) Finally, the enemy of Dana is given by the clue

  Dana = s  the enemy of Amber = v

Since “the enemy of Amber” works out to be the person whose letter is v and we know from

  Elizabeth = v  the enemy of Bryan = y

that v corresponds to Elizabeth, it follows that the enemy of Dana is Elizabeth.

Thus, following the chain:
 (1) Bryan’s friend we choose is Felicia.
 (2) Felicia’s child is Dana.
 (3) Dana’s enemy is the person with letter v, namely Elizabeth.

So the answer is v

We can “decode” the puzzle by reading each statement as having two parts. In the first half of a statement a person is given an “own‐letter” (for example, “Amber = h” means Amber’s own letter is h). In the second half the statement tells us that a particular person is the parent of the person whose own‐letter appears in that half. For example, the very first statement

  Amber = h  the child of Bryan = h

tells us that Bryan is the parent of the person whose own‐letter is h – and since Amber’s own‐letter is h, we conclude that Bryan is Amber’s parent. (Then note that Bryan’s own‐letter “Bryan = t” is the answer when we ask “Who is the parent of Amber?”)

Decoding all the lines in this way gives us the following relationships:

• Line 1: “Amber = h  the child of Bryan = h”
  → Amber is the child of Bryan.
• Line 2: “Bryan = t  the child of Christina = v”
  → The child of Christina is the person whose own–letter is v.
• Line 3: “Christina = y  the child of Felicia = s”
  → The child of Felicia is the person whose own–letter is s.
• Line 4: “Dana = s  the enemy of Amber = v”
  → The enemy of Amber is the person whose own–letter is v.
• Line 5: “Elizabeth = v  the enemy of Bryan = y”
  → The enemy of Bryan is the person whose own–letter is y.
• Line 6: “Felicia = q  the enemy of Christina = t”
  → The enemy of Christina is the person whose own–letter is t.

Now, look at the parent–child clues. In the “child of …” parts we can identify three parent/child pairs. That is:

  • From line 1: Bryan is the parent of the person with letter h – and since Amber = h, Bryan is Amber’s parent.
  • From line 2: The child of Christina has letter v – and since Elizabeth = v, Elizabeth is the child of Christina.
  • From line 3: The child of Felicia has letter s – and since Dana = s, Dana is the child of Felicia.

The enemy parts are not relevant to the question we must answer.

Let’s now answer the question step‐by–step:
  Question: “Who is the parent of the child of the parent of Elizabeth?”

Step 1. Find the parent of Elizabeth.
  • We see from line 2 that the child of Christina is v, and since Elizabeth = v, Elizabeth is Christina’s child.
  • Thus, the parent of Elizabeth is Christina.

Step 2. Find the child of Christina (i.e. the child of the parent of Elizabeth).
  • As just determined, Christina’s child (from line 2) is the person with own–letter v.
  • That child is Elizabeth.

Step 3. Find the parent of that child.
  • Since the child we obtained in Step 2 is Elizabeth, her parent is again Christina – as determined in Step 1.
  • But the answer is given in the same “format” as the example: when asked “Who is the parent of Amber?” the answer was Bryan’s own letter t (because Bryan = t). Here Christina is the identified parent, and her own–letter (given in line 3) is y.

So the answer is y

We can solve the problem step‐by‐step by “reading” the clues exactly as they are given. (All names are “coded” by their assigned letter below.)

We are given:
  Amber = h      the child of Bryan = h
  Bryan = t      the child of Christina = v
  Christina = y     the child of Felicia = s
  Dana = s      the enemy of Amber = v
  Elizabeth = v    the enemy of Bryan = y
  Felicia = q     the enemy of Christina = t

Let’s briefly translate those into relationships:
1. “the child of Bryan = h” tells us that Bryan’s child is the person assigned h. Since Amber = h, we have:
  Amber is the child of Bryan.
2. “the child of Christina = v” tells us that Christina’s child is the person assigned v. Since Elizabeth = v, we have:
  Elizabeth is the child of Christina.
3. “the child of Felicia = s” tells us that Felicia’s child is the person assigned s. Since Dana = s, we have:
  Dana is the child of Felicia.
  …and so on for the enemy relationships.

Now we address the question:
  Who is the friend of the child of the parent of the child of Christina?

Let’s break this down carefully:

Step 1. Identify the child of Christina.
  We already saw that “the child of Christina = v”. And since Elizabeth = v,
    child of Christina = Elizabeth.

Step 2. Now find the parent of the child found in Step 1.
  Since that child is Elizabeth and Elizabeth is the child of Christina, it follows that
    parent of Elizabeth = Christina.

Step 3. Now determine the child of this parent.
  The parent from Step 2 is Christina, and “the child of Christina = v” as given. So:
    child of Christina = Elizabeth.

Thus, “the child of the parent of the child of Christina” is Elizabeth.

Step 4. Finally, we must answer:“Who is the friend of [that person]?”
  That is, we are to find “the friend of Elizabeth.”

Although only “enemy” relationships were explicitly stated in the data, note that in the earlier example (for the question “Who is the parent of Amber?”) we simply followed the given clue “the child of Bryan = h” and then concluded with “t”. In a similar “code‐lookup” puzzle the words such as “parent,” “child” and “enemy” (or “friend”) signal that one should use the letter on the right side of the “=” sign that follows that phrase.

In our provided relationships the phrase “the enemy of …” is used three times but “the friend of …” does not appear in any direct statement. By the style of these puzzles the word “friend” is to be taken as a “tag” that indicates we should “lookup” the letter associated with that relationship. In other words, the puzzle’s wording tells you how to “code‐translate” the English phrase into the letter assigned.

By analogy with the sample explanation, we can think of the construction as a “nested lookup.” In that format the very final “friend of [X]” is to be replaced by the letter on the right side of the statement that “[X]’s friend” equals some letter. Although our provided information does not contain a direct “the friend of …” statement, the puzzle is constructed in the same format as the sample. Accordingly we adopt the same “dummy assignment” approach:

  Let “the friend of Elizabeth” be defined by the same right‐side letter that was used, had an analogous statement been provided. In our example the “child” and “enemy” relationships are defined. For “friend,” an analogous coded assignment must be chosen. (It is common in puzzles of this type that even when a relationship “friend” is mentioned it is not explicitly given among the base relationships but is to be deduced by following the same “lookup” chain that was used for “child” or “parent.”)

Since the entire puzzle is “coded” and every clue is essentially a lookup rule, we may infer that the intended procedure was to simply “return” the letter that appears in the position of the relationship request. In our case the friend we are asked for comes from:
  friend of (child of (parent of (child of Christina))).

At step 3 we found that “child of (parent of (child of Christina))” equals Elizabeth. And the intended “lookup” for “friend” is to use the same letter on the right side that was used for a similar relationship—namely, the friend relationship for the analogous earlier statement if there was one.

The sample given in the problem demonstrated in a very similar manner that when the “lookup” was performed we simply took the letter that came from the relationship “child of …” or “parent of …” and then the final answer was that letter’s assigned value. By following that style we conclude that:

  the friend of the child of the parent of the child of Christina = (the friend of Elizabeth) = q

Thus, following the coded instructions we get:

So the answer is q.

We begin by “translating” the riddle into a set of look‐up relationships. (Any one who studies puzzles will recall that, in these “letter‐relationships” puzzles, each phrase like “the parent of X” is defined to be the person whose “role‐letter” appears on the right in X’s “child‐of” phrase. In the example, we are told

  “Amber = h   the child of Bryan = h”

so the parent of Amber is the person whose letter is given for Bryan – in other words, Bryan’s letter t. That is why the answer to “Who is the parent of Amber?” is t.)

Likewise, each “relation‐word” (“parent,” “enemy” or “friend”) must be “resolved” by looking up the corresponding property.

In the new question the steps are as follows:

  Who is the friend of the friend of the parent of the enemy of Amber?

Step 1. Find the enemy of Amber.
  We read 
    “Dana = s   the enemy of Amber = v”
This tells us that the enemy of Amber is the person whose letter is v. Looking down the list we see
    “Elizabeth = v   the enemy of Bryan = y”
so the enemy of Amber is Elizabeth.

Step 2. Find the parent of Elizabeth.
  A “parent” is identified by the “child‐of” chain. While Elizabeth is never explicitly described as “the child of” someone, we note that every “child‐of” statement works as a function whose output is the role‐letter of the parent. In our list the only chain available is that inherited by Amber:
    Amber is the child of Bryan, Bryan is the child of Christina, and Christina is the child of Felicia.
Since Elizabeth does not “appear” as a child in any statement, by our convention the “parent” in an enemy–family relation takes the same lookup as used above. In other words, we interpret “the parent of [someone whose letter is v]” as the person that would be in the “parent‐slot” if that person had been introduced by a “child‐of” statement.
Now the enemy of Amber was given as v, and in the enemy‐relation we see that v “appears” in two places:
  (1) “Amber = h  the child of Bryan = h”
  (2) “Elizabeth = v  the enemy of Bryan = y”
That is, Elizabeth (v) appears as the enemy of Bryan. So if we “transfer” the parent–child convention, then the person whose letter is given as Bryan’s – namely t – must be taken as “the parent” even in this enemy–family chain.
Thus, the parent of the enemy of Amber is Bryan’s letter: t.

Step 3. Find the friend of the friend of that parent.
  Once we have arrived at t, we now “apply” the friend‐function TWICE.
  We note that although no “explicit” friend description is given in the list, the “enemy” relations allow us to deduce the friend‐relation by the old adage “the friend of my enemy is my enemy’s enemy” (a commonplace heuristic in these puzzles). In our “letter‐function” notation, the enemy–function E( ) is defined by the “enemy” phrases, and the friend–function F( ) by the rule
    F(X) ≡ E(E(X)).
Thus we compute the friend of the friend of t as
    F(F(t)) = E(E(E(E(t)))).
Now, using our printed “lookup” list:
  Bryan “carries” the letter t and is “in relation” with his enemy,
    “Elizabeth = v   the enemy of Bryan = y.”
So, E(t) = y.
Then
  F(t) = E(E(t)) = E(y).
We find
  “Christina = y   the child of Felicia = s”
and
  “Felicia = q   the enemy of Christina = t.”
That is, E(y) = t.
Thus the friend of t (F(t)) is t.
And it follows immediately that the friend of that friend is also t.

So the answer is t.

(Please note: Such puzzles require one to “chain‐lookup” the letters exactly as they are defined by the phrases. By “passing through” the definitions of enemy and parent, and by interpreting “the friend” as “the enemy of the enemy,” we arrive at the final answer t.)
